challenges.name: bulkheads-quiz
challenges.title: Read the report export incident
challenges.description: Three statements about how Rice Rocket's monthly report exports took checkout down, and how bulkheads change that. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Virtual threads remove one limit (platform threads). Look at the error: which other shared resource ran out?
Ask on which thread the protected call runs in each kind of bulkhead, and what the caller gets back: a result, or a CompletionStage.
Compare two ways to handle the third concurrent export: wait in a queue (for how long, holding what?) or fail at once with an answer the client can act on.

questions.question:
order-service runs on virtual threads, yet checkout failed while finance ran month-end exports:

```yaml
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
```

```text
18:02:11 POST /checkouts 500 HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms (total=10, active=10, idle=0, waiting=184)
18:02:11 GET /reports/orders.csv  ... 10 exports running, each holding a connection for ~4 min
```

Statement: "With virtual threads a slow endpoint can no longer starve the others, so a bulkhead around the report exports is unnecessary."
questions.explanation: False. Virtual threads make waiting cheap, so the platform-thread limit is gone, but the exports still held all 10 database connections; checkout queued for the pool and timed out after 30 s. Any shared, limited resource (connection pool, a partner's rate limit, memory) still needs a bulkhead: here, at most 2 concurrent exports so 8 connections stay for everything else.

False. A semaphore bulkhead only limits how many calls run at once; the call runs on the caller's own thread, which is blocked for the whole export. A thread-pool bulkhead hands the call to its own bounded pool and queue, and the method returns a CompletionStage. With virtual threads the semaphore type is usually enough: blocking the caller is cheap, and the limit is what protects the shared resource.

questions.question:
The export bulkhead is configured like this, and a third finance user starts an export while two are running:

```yaml
resilience4j.bulkhead.instances.reports:
  max-concurrent-calls: 2
  max-wait-duration: 0
```

```text
18:20:04 GET /reports/orders.csv 503 BulkheadFullException: Bulkhead 'reports' is full and does not permit further calls (2 ms)
         Retry-After: 120
```

Statement: "With max-wait-duration 0 the third export fails at once instead of queueing, which keeps request threads and connections free; the fallback should answer with something the user can act on, such as 503 with Retry-After."
questions.explanation: True. A wait of 0 rejects immediately when both permits are taken: the request does not hold a thread or a connection while it waits. A short wait (a few hundred ms) smooths small bursts; a long one turns the bulkhead into a slow queue. The fallback decides what the user sees: here a 503 with Retry-After, or an "export queued, we will email you" answer.

challenges.name: per-dependency-bulkheads
challenges.title: One bulkhead per dependency
challenges.description: order-service calls payments, couriers and the reporting database through one HTTP client and one pool; month-end exports took every slot and checkout failed. The editor holds `Main.java` with semaphore bulkheads modelled on Resilience4j's, their key blocks missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: each dependency has its own bulkhead with its own `max` and `wait`; a call takes a free permit, or waits in line for at most `wait` ms (rejected at once when `wait` is 0); a call that has waited `wait` ms without a permit is rejected at that moment; and every finished call, failed or not, gives its permit back so the oldest waiting call of that dependency can start. The test runner replays timed calls and prints when each started, finished or was rejected, and the peak concurrency per dependency.
hints: Draw a timeline per dependency: how many calls hold a permit at each moment, who is waiting since when, and what happens at the moment a call ends or a wait runs out?
Look at `computeIfAbsent` keyed by the dependency, the three cases in `arrive` (free permit, `maxWaitMs > 0`, reject), an unconditional `b.inUse--` in `finish`, and `w.deadline() > now` in `expire`.

A per-tenant limit for an export worker: `Limit l = limits.computeIfAbsent(tenant, t -> new Limit(config.get(t)));` then `if (l.active < l.max) { l.active++; run(job); } else if (l.waitMs > 0) l.queue.add(new Queued(job, now + l.waitMs)); else reject(job);`, `finally { l.active--; }`, and `l.queue.removeIf(q -> q.deadline <= now && reject(q.job));`.
